decks.title: Ionic Equilibrium — Part 1: Electrolytes, acid–base concepts, Ostwald's dilution law
goals: Classify substances as strong, weak or non-electrolytes and explain the degree of ionisation
Apply the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts and identify conjugate acid–base pairs
Derive Ostwald's dilution law, use Ka and Kb to compare strengths, and write the stages of ionisation of a polybasic acid

slides.heading: Why does one acid conduct better than another?
slides.body_md: Part 1: some solutes fill water with ions and others give almost none. We classify **electrolytes**, meet three **concepts of acids and bases**, and derive **Ostwald's dilution law**.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 1

slides.narration: Welcome to Part One of ionic equilibrium. Some substances fill water with ions, while others give almost none, and that decides how well the solution conducts. We classify electrolytes, study three ways of defining acids and bases, derive the dilution law of Ostwald, and compare the strengths of acids and bases.

slides.heading: Strong, weak and non-electrolytes
slides.body_md: An **electrolyte** conducts electricity in solution through its **ions**. A **strong electrolyte** is almost completely ionised; a **weak electrolyte** is only slightly ionised, so **molecules and ions are in equilibrium**; a **non-electrolyte** gives no ions.

visual.alt: Table of strong, weak and non-electrolytes with examples

slides.narration: An electrolyte conducts electricity in solution because of its ions. A strong electrolyte, such as hydrochloric acid or sodium hydroxide, is almost completely ionised. A weak electrolyte, such as ethanoic acid, is only slightly ionised, so molecules and ions stay in equilibrium. A non-electrolyte, such as glucose, forms no ions at all.

slides.heading: What a bulb tells us
slides.body_md: Conductance depends on the **number of ions per litre**. In the strong electrolyte every unit is ionised; in the weak one only a small fraction is; the non-electrolyte stays as **neutral molecules**.

slides.heading: Degree of ionisation
slides.body_md: The **degree of ionisation** α is the **fraction of the dissolved electrolyte present as ions**: α = amount ionised ÷ amount dissolved. For strong electrolytes α ≈ 1; for weak ones α is small. A weak electrolyte HA gives $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha$ at concentration C.

headers: Effect on α of a weak electrolyte
rows: a stronger acid or base has a larger α
a solvent of high dielectric constant (water) favours ionisation

visual.alt: Table of the factors that affect the degree of ionisation

slides.narration: The degree of ionisation is the fraction of the dissolved electrolyte that is present as ions. For a strong electrolyte it is close to one, and for a weak one it is small. It depends on the nature of the electrolyte and the solvent, it rises with temperature, and it increases when the solution is diluted.

slides.heading: Three concepts of acids and bases
slides.body_md: The **Arrhenius** concept needs water: an acid gives H⁺, a base gives OH⁻. **Brønsted–Lowry** widens it: an acid is a **proton donor** and a base a **proton acceptor**. **Lewis** widens it further: an acid is an **electron-pair acceptor** and a base an **electron-pair donor**.

rows: only aqueous solutions; NH₃ has no OH group
includes acids with no hydrogen (BF₃, AlCl₃)

visual.alt: Table comparing the Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry and Lewis concepts of acids and bases

slides.narration: There are three concepts of acids and bases. Arrhenius says an acid gives hydrogen ions in water and a base gives hydroxide ions, which limits it to water. Brønsted and Lowry say an acid donates a proton and a base accepts one. Lewis goes furthest: an acid accepts an electron pair and a base donates one.

slides.heading: Conjugate acid–base pairs
slides.body_md: When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its **conjugate base**; when a base accepts a proton, it becomes its **conjugate acid**. The two members of a pair differ by **one proton**. The **stronger** the acid, the **weaker** its conjugate base. **Water** is **amphiprotic**: it can act as acid or base.

visual.alt: Table of acids with their conjugate bases and bases with their conjugate acids

slides.narration: When an acid gives away a proton, the species left behind is its conjugate base. When a base takes up a proton, it becomes its conjugate acid. The two members of a pair differ by exactly one proton. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. Water can act as an acid or as a base, so it is amphiprotic.

slides.heading: Worked example: conjugate pairs in a reaction
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs in $\ce{H2S + NH3 <=> HS- + NH4+}$.

$\ce{H2S}$ donates a proton, so it is the acid and $\ce{HS-}$ is its conjugate base. $\ce{NH3}$ accepts a proton, so it is the base and $\ce{NH4+}$ is its conjugate acid.

visual.alt: Table of the two conjugate acid-base pairs in the reaction of hydrogen sulphide with ammonia

slides.narration: Look for the species that loses a proton. Hydrogen sulphide gives away a proton, so it is the acid, and what remains, the hydrosulphide ion, is its conjugate base. Ammonia gains a proton, so it is the base, and the ammonium ion is its conjugate acid. Each pair differs by one proton.

slides.heading: Quick check: limits of a definition
slides.body_md: Which concept defines a base as a substance that produces hydroxide ions?
slides.narration: Quick check. Ammonia is a base even though its molecule has no hydroxide group. Decide which definition of a base this fact contradicts, and which other definitions still include ammonia as a base.

slides.heading: A Lewis acid and a Lewis base
slides.body_md: In **NH₃ + BF₃** the lone pair on nitrogen is **donated** to boron, which has only six electrons. A **coordinate bond** forms and no proton is transferred, so this is a **Lewis** reaction but not a Brønsted one.

slides.heading: Lewis acids and Lewis bases
slides.body_md: A **Lewis acid** has an empty orbital or incomplete octet; a **Lewis base** has a lone pair. Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base, because it must donate a lone pair to the proton, but **Lewis acids include species with no hydrogen**.

visual.alt: Table of examples of Lewis acids and Lewis bases

slides.narration: A Lewis acid has an empty orbital or an incomplete octet, and so it accepts an electron pair. A Lewis base has a lone pair to donate. A proton, boron trifluoride, aluminium chloride and metal ions are Lewis acids. Ammonia, water, hydroxide, chloride and cyanide ions are Lewis bases.

slides.heading: Ostwald's dilution law: derivation
slides.body_md: For $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$ at concentration C and degree of ionisation α, the equilibrium amounts are **C(1 − α), Cα, Cα**. So $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$. For a **weak** acid α ≪ 1, so **Ka = Cα²** and **α = √(Ka/C)**. Then $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = \sqrt{K_aC}$. A weak base gives $\alpha = \sqrt{K_b/C}$.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the derivation of Ostwald dilution law

slides.narration: Start with the acid at concentration C and degree of ionisation alpha. At equilibrium the acid is C times one minus alpha, and each ion is C times alpha. Putting these in the expression gives the ionisation constant as C alpha squared over one minus alpha. For a weak acid alpha is small, so alpha equals the square root of the constant over C.

slides.heading: Degree of ionisation against concentration
slides.body_md: The curves follow $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ (exact quadratic used). On **dilution α increases**, and at any concentration the acid with the **larger Ka** has the **larger α**. α tends to 1 only at very high dilution.

slides.heading: Worked example: degree of ionisation of ethanoic acid
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find α, $[\text{H}^+]$ and pH of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid, $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$.

$\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C} = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-5}/0.10} = 0.0134$ (about 1.3%); $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = 1.34 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹; pH $= 2.87$.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the degree of ionisation and pH of ethanoic acid

slides.narration: Divide the ionisation constant by the concentration and take the square root, which gives a degree of ionisation of about one point three percent. Multiply by the concentration to get the hydrogen ion concentration, about one point three times ten to the minus three. The pH is the negative logarithm of that, about two point nine.

slides.heading: Quick check: dilution law
slides.body_md: Use α = √(Ka/C): what happens to α when C is divided by 4?
slides.narration: Quick check. A weak monobasic acid is diluted to a quarter of its concentration at constant temperature. Use the square root relation between the degree of ionisation and the concentration to decide by what factor the degree of ionisation changes.

slides.heading: Ka, Kb and the strength of acids and bases
slides.body_md: A **larger Ka** means a **stronger acid**, a larger α at the same concentration and a **smaller pKa** (pKa = −log Ka). The same holds for **Kb** and bases. At equal concentration $[\text{H}^+] = \sqrt{K_aC}$, so the strength order follows the order of Ka.

visual.alt: Table of the ionisation constants, pKa and degrees of ionisation of five weak acids

slides.narration: A larger ionisation constant means a stronger acid. Such an acid has a smaller value of the negative logarithm of its constant, and a larger degree of ionisation at the same concentration. Nitrous acid is the strongest in this table and hydrocyanic acid is the weakest. The same reasoning applies to the ionisation constants of bases.

slides.heading: Polybasic acids ionise in stages
slides.body_md: A **polybasic acid** gives up its protons **one stage at a time**, each with its own constant: **Ka1 ≫ Ka2 ≫ Ka3**. The next proton must leave a **negative ion**, which holds it more strongly, and H⁺ already present holds back further ionisation.

visual.alt: Table of the three stages of ionisation of phosphoric acid

slides.narration: A polybasic acid gives up its protons in stages, and each stage has its own ionisation constant. Phosphoric acid has three stages. Each constant is far smaller than the one before, because a proton must leave an ion that is already negatively charged, and because hydrogen ions from the first stage hold back the next. So the first stage supplies almost all the hydrogen ions.

slides.heading: Phosphoric acid on a pKa scale
slides.body_md: The pKa values are **2.12, 7.21 and 12.32**. Each step is about **10⁵ times weaker** than the previous one, so in a solution of H₃PO₄ the species present in quantity are **H₃PO₄, H₂PO₄⁻ and H⁺**; HPO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are present only in traces.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Strong electrolytes are fully ionised, weak ones partly (equilibrium), non-electrolytes give no ions; α is the fraction ionised.
Arrhenius: H⁺ and OH⁻ in water; Brønsted–Lowry: proton donor and acceptor; Lewis: electron-pair acceptor and donor.
Conjugate pairs differ by one proton; the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base.
Ostwald: Ka = Cα² / (1 − α); for weak electrolytes α = √(Ka/C), so α rises on dilution; [H⁺] = √(KaC).
Polybasic acids ionise in stages with Ka1 ≫ Ka2 ≫ Ka3.

visual.alt: Summary table of the key ideas of Part 1

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part One. Strong electrolytes are completely ionised and weak ones only partly. We met three definitions of acids and bases, and conjugate pairs that differ by one proton. The dilution law of Ostwald shows that for a weak electrolyte the degree of ionisation equals the square root of the constant over the concentration. Polybasic acids ionise stage by stage.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: In the derivation write the three equilibrium amounts first, then Ka, then the approximation α ≪ 1.
Name both members of a conjugate pair and say which is the acid and which the base; water can be either.
Use α = √(Ka/C) only for weak electrolytes with small α; otherwise solve Ka = Cα² / (1 − α).
For a polybasic acid write each stage separately with its own Ka.
Classify BF₃ and AlCl₃ as Lewis acids and NH₃ and CN⁻ as Lewis bases, with the electron-pair reason.

rows: α increases; the ionisation constant stays the same
Writing H₃PO₄ → 3H⁺ + PO₄³⁻ in one step

decks.title: Ionic Equilibrium — Part 2: Kw, pH and pOH, indicators and titrations
goals: Use the ionic product of water, pH, pOH and pKw, also at temperatures other than 298 K
Calculate the pH of strong and weak acids and bases and of mixtures of a strong acid and a strong base
Explain how indicators work and choose a suitable indicator for each type of titration

slides.heading: How acidic is a solution?
slides.body_md: Part 2: water itself ionises a little. That fact gives the **ionic product Kw**, the **pH scale**, and a way to choose an **indicator** for a titration.

visual.alt: Flow chart of the topics of Part 2

slides.narration: Welcome to Part Two. Pure water ionises very slightly, and this fact leads to the ionic product of water and the pH scale. We calculate the pH of strong and weak acids and bases, and of mixtures. Then we study indicators and learn how to choose the right one for each kind of titration.

slides.heading: Ionic product of water and temperature
slides.body_md: Water ionises slightly: $\ce{2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-}$. The **ionic product** is $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]$, **1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² L⁻² at 298 K**. The ionisation is **endothermic**, so Kw **rises with temperature**. Pure water is always **neutral** ([H⁺] = [OH⁻]) but its pH is not always 7.

visual.alt: Table of the ionic product of water, pKw and the pH of pure water at four temperatures

slides.narration: Water ionises slightly, and the product of the hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations is the ionic product, which is one times ten to the minus fourteen at room temperature. The ionisation absorbs heat, so the product rises with temperature. Pure water stays neutral because the two concentrations are equal, but its pH falls below seven when it is warm.

slides.heading: pH, pOH and pKw
slides.body_md: **pH = −log [H⁺]**, **pOH = −log [OH⁻]** and **pKw = −log Kw**, so **pH + pOH = pKw** (14.00 at 298 K). Each unit of pH is a **factor of 10** in [H⁺]. At 298 K a solution is acidic below pH 7 and basic above.

visual.alt: Table linking pH with the hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations

slides.narration: The pH is the negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration, and the pOH is the same for hydroxide ions. Together they add up to the negative logarithm of the ionic product, which is fourteen at room temperature. Each step of one pH unit means the hydrogen ion concentration changes by a factor of ten.

slides.heading: Quick check: the logarithmic scale
slides.body_md: A difference of n pH units is a factor of 10ⁿ in [H⁺].
slides.narration: Quick check. Two liquids differ in pH by a few units. Because the scale is logarithmic, the ratio of their hydrogen ion concentrations is ten raised to the difference. Work out the ratio for the two liquids in the question and choose the matching option.

slides.heading: Worked example: pH of a strong base
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the pH of 0.0030 mol L⁻¹ calcium hydroxide at 298 K (completely ionised).

$\ce{Ca(OH)2 -> Ca^2+ + 2OH-}$, so $[\text{OH}^-] = 2 \times 0.0030 = 0.006$ mol L⁻¹; pOH $= 2.22$; pH $= 14.00 - 2.22 = 11.78$.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the pH of calcium hydroxide solution

slides.narration: Calcium hydroxide is a strong base that releases two hydroxide ions per formula unit, so the hydroxide concentration is twice the concentration of the base. Take the negative logarithm to get the pOH, which is about two point two. Subtract it from fourteen to obtain a pH of about eleven point eight.

slides.heading: pH of weak acids and weak bases
slides.body_md: For a weak monobasic acid, $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = \sqrt{K_aC}$; for a weak base, $[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_bC}$, then pOH and pH = 14 − pOH. This needs **α ≪ 1**. Do **not** treat a weak electrolyte as fully ionised.

visual.alt: Table of formulas for the pH of weak acids and weak bases

slides.narration: For a weak acid the hydrogen ion concentration is the square root of the ionisation constant times the concentration, provided the degree of ionisation is small. For a weak base the same expression gives the hydroxide ion concentration, and we then find the pOH and subtract from fourteen to get the pH.

slides.heading: Worked example: pH of a weak base
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the pH of 0.20 mol L⁻¹ methylamine, $K_b = 4.4 \times 10^{-4}$ at 298 K, taking α ≪ 1.

$[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_bC} = \sqrt{4.4 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.20} = 9.38 \times 10^{-3}$ mol L⁻¹; pOH $= 2.03$; pH $= 11.97$. (α = 0.047, small enough.)

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the pH of methylamine solution

slides.narration: Multiply the base ionisation constant by the concentration and take the square root, giving a hydroxide ion concentration of about nine point four times ten to the minus three. Its negative logarithm is the pOH, about two. Subtract from fourteen to get a pH of about twelve. The degree of ionisation is under five percent, so the approximation holds.

slides.heading: Quick check: pH of a weak acid
slides.body_md: Square root of Ka times C, then the negative logarithm.
slides.narration: Quick check. For a weak acid assume the degree of ionisation is small. Multiply the ionisation constant by the concentration, take the square root to get the hydrogen ion concentration, and then the negative logarithm. Match your answer with the options.

slides.heading: Mixing a strong acid with a strong base
slides.body_md: Compare the **moles** of H⁺ and OH⁻ (concentration × volume), not the concentrations. The **excess** is divided by the **total volume**. If H⁺ is in excess, pH = −log [H⁺]; if OH⁻ is in excess, find pOH, then pH = 14 − pOH.

nodes.label: pH or pOH; use pH + pOH = 14

visual.alt: Flow chart of the steps for the pH of a mixture of a strong acid and a strong base

slides.narration: To find the pH of a mixture of a strong acid and a strong base, first work out the moles of each ion. Subtract the smaller from the larger to find the excess. Divide the excess by the total volume of the mixture. Then take the negative logarithm, and if the base is in excess, subtract the pOH from fourteen.

slides.heading: Worked example: a mixture
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Find the pH when 30.0 mL of 0.120 mol L⁻¹ nitric acid is mixed with 20.0 mL of 0.060 mol L⁻¹ potassium hydroxide at 298 K.

$n(\text{H}^+) = 3.6$ mmol, $n(\text{OH}^-) = 1.2$ mmol; excess H⁺ $= 2.4$ mmol in 50.0 mL, so $[\text{H}^+] = 0.048$ mol L⁻¹ and pH $= 1.32$.

visual.alt: Table of the calculation of the pH of a mixture of nitric acid and potassium hydroxide

slides.narration: First the moles. The acid supplies three point six millimoles of hydrogen ions and the base supplies one point two millimoles of hydroxide ions. The acid is in excess by two point four millimoles. Dividing by the total volume of fifty millilitres gives a hydrogen ion concentration of about forty eight thousandths, so the pH is about one point three.

slides.heading: Acid–base indicators
slides.body_md: An **indicator** is a weak organic acid or base whose **ionised and un-ionised forms have different colours**. The colour changes over a **narrow pH range** of about two units; only a **few drops** are used, since the indicator itself consumes a little acid or alkali.

visual.alt: Table of the pH ranges and colours of four indicators

slides.narration: An indicator is a weak organic acid or base whose ionised and un-ionised forms have different colours. Its colour changes over a narrow range of pH, about two units wide. Methyl orange changes in acid, bromothymol blue near neutral, and phenolphthalein in alkaline solution. Only a few drops are added, because the indicator itself uses up some acid or alkali.

slides.heading: Titration curves and indicator ranges
slides.body_md: Each curve shows pH against titrant added to **25.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹** solution; the **shaded bands** are indicator ranges. An indicator is suitable if its band lies on the **steep rise** of the curve. The strong acid–strong base rise spans pH 4 to 10; the other two rises are shorter and lie above or below 7.

A weak acid with a strong base ends above seven, so phenolphthalein is the right choice. A strong acid with a weak base ends below seven, so methyl orange or methyl red is used. notes.title: Ionic Equilibrium: Acids, Bases and pH — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Strong, weak and non-electrolytes; degree of ionisation
sections.body_md:
An **electrolyte** conducts electricity in solution because it gives **ions**. A **strong electrolyte** (HCl, HNO₃, NaOH, KNO₃) is practically completely ionised; a **weak electrolyte** (CH₃COOH, NH₄OH, H₂CO₃) is only partly ionised, so ions and molecules are in equilibrium; a **non-electrolyte** (glucose, urea, sucrose) gives no ions.

The **degree of ionisation** α is the fraction of the dissolved electrolyte present as ions: α = amount ionised ÷ amount dissolved. For a weak acid HA of concentration C, $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha$. α depends on the nature of the electrolyte and solvent, rises with temperature and **increases on dilution**.

sections.heading: 2. Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts; conjugate pairs
sections.body_md:
**Arrhenius:** an acid gives H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water, a base gives OH⁻; limited to aqueous solutions and to bases with OH groups. **Brønsted–Lowry:** an acid is a **proton donor**, a base a **proton acceptor**. **Lewis:** an acid is an **electron-pair acceptor** (H⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, Cu²⁺), a base an **electron-pair donor** (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, CN⁻).

A **conjugate pair** differs by one proton: acid ⇌ base + H⁺. The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. **Water** is **amphiprotic**. Example: in $\ce{H2S + NH3 <=> HS- + NH4+}$ the pairs are H₂S / HS⁻ and NH₄⁺ / NH₃.

key_terms.definition_md: An acid and the base formed when it loses one proton.
Able to act both as a Brønsted acid and as a Brønsted base, like water.

A covalent bond in which both electrons come from one atom.

sections.heading: 3. Ostwald's dilution law (derivation)
sections.body_md:
For $\text{HA} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^+ + \text{A}^-$ with concentration C and degree of ionisation α, the equilibrium amounts are C(1 − α), Cα and Cα. So

$K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} = \dfrac{C\alpha \cdot C\alpha}{C(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$.

For a weak electrolyte α ≪ 1, so $K_a = C\alpha^2$, $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ and $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = \sqrt{K_aC}$. A weak base gives $\alpha = \sqrt{K_b/C}$ and $[\text{OH}^-] = \sqrt{K_bC}$. Hence α increases as C decreases (on dilution), while Ka depends only on temperature. Example: 0.050 mol L⁻¹ methanoic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$) has α ≈ 0.060 and $[\text{H}^+] \approx$ 3.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹.

sections.heading: 4. Acid strength, Ka and Kb; polybasic acids
sections.body_md:
A larger Ka (or Kb) means a stronger acid (or base), a larger α at the same concentration and a smaller pKa = −log Ka. At 298 K: Ka(HNO₂) = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴, Ka(HCOOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴, Ka(C₆H₅COOH) = 6.5 × 10⁻⁵, Ka(CH₃COOH) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, Ka(HCN) = 4.9 × 10⁻¹⁰; Kb(NH₃) = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵.

A **polybasic acid** ionises in stages, each with its own constant. H₃PO₄ ⇌ H⁺ + H₂PO₄⁻ (Ka1 = 7.5 × 10⁻³); H₂PO₄⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + HPO₄²⁻ (Ka2 = 6.2 × 10⁻⁸); HPO₄²⁻ ⇌ H⁺ + PO₄³⁻ (Ka3 = 4.8 × 10⁻¹³). Ka1 ≫ Ka2 ≫ Ka3, because a proton leaves a negative ion less easily and the H⁺ already present holds back later stages; almost all the H⁺ comes from the first stage.

key_terms.definition_md: The negative logarithm of Ka; a smaller pKa means a stronger acid.
An acid that can donate more than one proton per molecule, in stages.

sections.heading: 5. Ionic product of water; pH, pOH and pKw
sections.body_md:
Water ionises slightly: $\ce{2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-}$ and $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]$ = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² L⁻² at 298 K. Ionisation is endothermic, so Kw increases with temperature (about 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 323 K). **pH = −log [H⁺], pOH = −log [OH⁻], pKw = −log Kw** and **pH + pOH = pKw** (14.00 at 298 K). A neutral solution has [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so its pH = ½ pKw (6.63 at 323 K).

**Calculations.** Strong acid: [H⁺] = C (×2 for H₂SO₄ if both protons are counted). Strong base: [OH⁻] = C (×2 for Ca(OH)₂, Ba(OH)₂). Weak acid or base: [H⁺] = √(KaC) or [OH⁻] = √(KbC). Mixture of a strong acid and a strong base: excess moles ÷ total volume. Example: 0.050 mol L⁻¹ strong acid, pH = 1.30; 0.050 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid, pH = 3.02.

key_terms.definition_md: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻], the product of the ion concentrations in water or any dilute aqueous solution at a given temperature.
The negative logarithm (base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol L⁻¹.

sections.heading: 6. Acid–base indicators and their choice in titrations
sections.body_md:
An **indicator** is a weak organic acid or base whose ionised and un-ionised forms have different colours; the colour changes over a narrow pH range (about two units) and only a few drops are used. Ranges: methyl orange 3.1–4.4 (red to yellow), methyl red 4.4–6.2 (red to yellow), bromothymol blue 6.0–7.6 (yellow to blue), phenolphthalein 8.3–10.0 (colourless to pink).

**Choice:** the indicator range must lie on the steep part of the titration curve. Strong acid–strong base (steep rise about pH 4 to 10): any of the four. Weak acid–strong base (equivalence about pH 8.7 for 0.1 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid): phenolphthalein. Strong acid–weak base (equivalence about pH 5.3): methyl orange or methyl red. Weak acid–weak base: no sharp rise, so no ordinary indicator.

key_terms.definition_md: A weak organic acid or base whose two forms have different colours, used to detect the end point of a titration.
The stage at which the acid and base have been mixed in exactly equivalent amounts.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying α decreases on dilution, or that Ka changes with concentration (it depends only on temperature).
- Writing the derivation without the equilibrium amounts C(1 − α), Cα, Cα, or forgetting the approximation α ≪ 1.
- Using pH + pOH = 14 at a temperature other than 298 K, or forgetting that pure water is neutral at pH ½ pKw.
- Not doubling [OH⁻] for Ca(OH)₂ and Ba(OH)₂, or dividing by one volume instead of the total volume in mixtures.
- Naming phenolphthalein for a strong acid titrated with a weak base.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Derivation of Ostwald's law: equilibrium amounts (1), Ka expression (1), approximation and α = √(Ka/C) (1).
- pH calculations: [H⁺] or [OH⁻] (1), logarithm step (1), final pH with two decimals.
- Conjugate pairs and Lewis acids or bases: each pair or species with its reason.
- Indicator choice: pH at equivalence (1), range matched to the steep part (1).

cards.front_md: What is an electrolyte?
cards.back_md: A substance whose solution conducts electricity because it contains ions.

cards.front_md: Give two strong and two weak electrolytes.
cards.back_md: Strong: HCl, NaOH. Weak: CH₃COOH, NH₄OH.

cards.front_md: Why does a glucose solution not conduct?
cards.back_md: Glucose is a non-electrolyte: it stays as neutral molecules and gives no ions.

cards.front_md: Define degree of ionisation.
cards.back_md: The fraction of the dissolved electrolyte present as ions at equilibrium.

cards.front_md: How does α change on dilution?
cards.back_md: It increases.

cards.front_md: Arrhenius definitions of acid and base?
cards.back_md: Acid: gives H⁺ in water. Base: gives OH⁻ in water.

cards.front_md: Brønsted–Lowry definitions?
cards.back_md: Acid: proton donor. Base: proton acceptor.

cards.front_md: Lewis definitions?
cards.back_md: Acid: electron-pair acceptor. Base: electron-pair donor.

cards.front_md: What is a conjugate acid–base pair?
cards.back_md: Two species that differ by one proton, such as NH₄⁺ and NH₃.

cards.front_md: Conjugate base of H₂SO₄? Of HSO₄⁻?
cards.back_md: HSO₄⁻; SO₄²⁻.

cards.front_md: Conjugate acid of NH₃? Of H₂O?
cards.back_md: NH₄⁺; H₃O⁺.

cards.front_md: Why is water amphiprotic?
cards.back_md: It can donate a proton (to NH₃) and accept one (from HCl).

cards.front_md: Why is BF₃ a Lewis acid?
cards.back_md: Boron has an incomplete octet, so BF₃ accepts an electron pair (for example from NH₃).

cards.front_md: Two Lewis bases?
cards.back_md: NH₃ and OH⁻ (or H₂O, Cl⁻, CN⁻): each has a lone pair to donate.

cards.front_md: Limitation of the Arrhenius concept?
cards.back_md: It applies only to aqueous solutions and needs OH⁻ from the base itself (NH₃ has no OH group).

cards.front_md: Ostwald's dilution law for a weak acid?
cards.back_md: $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$, and $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$ for small α.

cards.front_md: Equilibrium amounts for HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻ in the derivation?
cards.back_md: C(1 − α) for HA, Cα for H⁺ and Cα for A⁻.

cards.front_md: [H⁺] of a weak monobasic acid?
cards.back_md: $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = \sqrt{K_aC}$

cards.front_md: If C falls to C/4, how does α change?
cards.back_md: It doubles, since α ∝ 1/√C.

cards.front_md: What does Ka depend on?
cards.back_md: Temperature only.

cards.front_md: Larger Ka means what for pKa and strength?
cards.back_md: Smaller pKa and a stronger acid.

cards.front_md: Write the first stage of ionisation of H₃PO₄ and its Ka.
cards.back_md: H₃PO₄ ⇌ H⁺ + H₂PO₄⁻, Ka1 = 7.5 × 10⁻³.

cards.front_md: Why is Ka2 much smaller than Ka1?
cards.back_md: A proton must leave a negative ion, which holds it more strongly; H⁺ from stage one also holds back stage two.

cards.front_md: State the ionic product of water at 298 K.
cards.back_md: Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² L⁻² at 298 K.

cards.front_md: Why does Kw increase with temperature?
cards.back_md: The ionisation of water is endothermic.

cards.front_md: Relation between pH, pOH and pKw?
cards.back_md: $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = \text{p}K_w$ (14.00 at 298 K).

cards.front_md: pH of pure water at a temperature where Kw = 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴?
cards.back_md: ½ pKw = 6.63: still neutral because [H⁺] = [OH⁻].

cards.front_md: How many times does [H⁺] change per pH unit?
cards.back_md: By a factor of 10.

cards.front_md: What is an acid–base indicator?
cards.back_md: A weak organic acid or base whose ionised and un-ionised forms differ in colour.

cards.front_md: Indicator for a weak acid titrated with a strong base?
cards.back_md: Phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0); equivalence about pH 8.7 for 0.1 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid.

cards.front_md: Indicator for a strong acid titrated with a weak base?
cards.back_md: Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) or methyl red (4.4–6.2); equivalence below pH 7.

cards.front_md: Why is no indicator suitable for a weak acid against a weak base?
cards.back_md: The curve has no steep rise at the equivalence point.

questions.stem_md: A student tests the conductivity of four 0.1 mol L⁻¹ aqueous solutions with a bulb and battery. Which solute is a non-electrolyte, so that the bulb stays dark?

options.text_md: sodium chloride
urea (carbamide)
ethanoic acid
ammonium hydroxide

questions.solution_md: Urea dissolves as molecules and gives no ions, so the solution does not conduct. Sodium chloride is a strong electrolyte; ethanoic acid and ammonium hydroxide are weak electrolytes that give a few ions — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which pair consists of one strong electrolyte and one weak electrolyte in water?

options.text_md: sodium hydroxide and potassium chloride
nitric acid and aqueous ammonia
ethanoic acid and carbonic acid
glucose and urea

questions.solution_md: Nitric acid is completely ionised (strong); aqueous ammonia is only slightly ionised (weak). The other pairs are strong + strong, weak + weak, and non-electrolyte + non-electrolyte — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of a weak monobasic acid in a school laboratory is found to be 1.5% ionised. The hydrogen ion concentration is:

options.text_md: 1.5 × 10⁻² mol L⁻¹
1.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹
1.5 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹
0.10 mol L⁻¹

questions.stem_md: The degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte such as ethanoic acid in water increases when:

options.text_md: the solution is cooled at constant concentration
more of the acid is dissolved in the same volume
the pressure above the solution is raised
the solution is diluted at constant temperature

questions.solution_md: On dilution there is more solvent per molecule of acid, and a larger fraction ionises (Ostwald's dilution law, α ∝ 1/√C). More acid in the same volume lowers α, cooling lowers it slightly, and pressure has no effect on a solution — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** At the same concentration, aqueous hydrochloric acid is a better conductor of electricity than aqueous ethanoic acid.

**Reason (R):** Hydrochloric acid is completely ionised in water and so gives many more ions per litre.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Conductance depends on the number of ions; HCl is a strong electrolyte (α ≈ 1) while ethanoic acid is weak (α ≈ 0.01 at 0.1 mol L⁻¹), and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? An aqueous solution of glucose conducts electricity because glucose molecules ionise in water to a small extent.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Glucose is a non-electrolyte: it dissolves as neutral molecules and gives no ions, so its solution does not conduct.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between a strong electrolyte and a weak electrolyte in water, giving one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A strong electrolyte is completely (or almost completely) ionised in aqueous solution, so there are no molecules of it in solution (for example HCl, NaOH, NaCl). A weak electrolyte is ionised only to a small extent, so molecules and ions are in equilibrium (for example CH₃COOH, NH₄OH).

questions.solution_md: Strong: fully ionised (HCl); weak: partly ionised, equilibrium with molecules (CH₃COOH).

marking_scheme.step: Strong electrolyte: complete ionisation, with an example
Weak electrolyte: partial ionisation and equilibrium, with an example

questions.stem_md: Define the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte. State three factors on which it depends, and say how it changes with each.

answer.model_answer_md: The degree of ionisation α is the fraction of the total number of moles of the electrolyte that is present as ions at equilibrium (α = moles ionised / moles dissolved). It depends on (i) the nature of the electrolyte (a stronger acid has a larger α), (ii) the concentration: α increases on dilution, and (iii) the temperature: α increases as the temperature rises. The nature of the solvent also matters (a solvent of high dielectric constant such as water increases α).

questions.solution_md: α = fraction ionised; depends on nature, concentration (increases on dilution), temperature (increases).

marking_scheme.step: Definition of α as a fraction
Dilution increases α, with the reason or the law
Nature of the electrolyte and temperature effects

questions.stem_md:
(a) A student has aqueous solutions of HCl, glucose, NH₄OH, NaOH, CH₃COOH, urea and KNO₃. Classify them as strong electrolytes, weak electrolytes and non-electrolytes. [2]

(b) Define the degree of ionisation and state two factors that change it. [1]

(c) A 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of a weak monobasic acid HA is 2.0% ionised (given). Calculate $[\text{H}^+]$ and the ionisation constant $K_a$, using $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Strong: HCl, NaOH, KNO₃. Weak: NH₄OH, CH₃COOH. Non-electrolytes: glucose, urea.

(b) The degree of ionisation is the fraction of the dissolved electrolyte present as ions at equilibrium; it depends on the nature of the electrolyte, the concentration (increases on dilution) and the temperature.

(c) [H⁺] = Cα = 0.050 × 0.020 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹. K_a = Cα² / (1 − α) = 0.050 × (0.020)² / 0.98 = 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ (about 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ using 1 − α ≈ 1).

marking_scheme.step: (a) Weak electrolytes and non-electrolytes correctly placed

questions.stem_md: In an aqueous solution of sodium carbonate, the carbonate ion accepts a proton from water. The conjugate acid of the carbonate ion is:

options.text_md: $\ce{H2CO3}$
$\ce{HCO3-}$
$\ce{CO2}$
$\ce{OH-}$

questions.solution_md: The conjugate acid of a base is the species formed when the base gains one proton: CO₃²⁻ + H⁺ gives HCO₃⁻ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In which of the following reactions in water does water act as a Brønsted acid?

options.text_md: $\ce{HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-}$
$\ce{CH3COOH + H2O <=> CH3COO- + H3O+}$
$\ce{H2S + H2O <=> HS- + H3O+}$
$\ce{NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH-}$

questions.solution_md: A Brønsted acid donates a proton. In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ water gives a proton to NH₃. In the other three reactions water accepts a proton to form H₃O⁺, so it is a base — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Anhydrous aluminium chloride dissolves in an inert, dry organic solvent that contains chloride ions: $\ce{AlCl3 + Cl- -> AlCl4-}$. In this reaction aluminium chloride acts as:

options.text_md: a Lewis base, since it donates an electron pair to the chloride ion
a Brønsted acid, since it donates a proton to the chloride ion
a Brønsted base, since it accepts a proton from the chloride ion
a Lewis acid, since it accepts an electron pair from the chloride ion

questions.solution_md: AlCl₃ has an incomplete octet on aluminium and accepts a lone pair from Cl⁻, forming a coordinate bond. An electron-pair acceptor is a Lewis acid; no proton is transferred, so the Brønsted terms do not apply — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A student reads that ammonia is a base although its molecule contains no hydroxide group. This is a limitation of the:

options.text_md: Arrhenius concept, which defines a base as a substance giving OH⁻ ions in water
Brønsted–Lowry concept, which defines a base as a proton acceptor
Lewis concept, which defines a base as an electron-pair donor
Brønsted–Lowry concept, which requires the base to contain hydrogen

questions.solution_md: The Arrhenius definition needs OH⁻ to be produced by the base itself, and is limited to aqueous solutions. Ammonia is a Brønsted base (accepts H⁺) and a Lewis base (donates a lone pair) — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Consider the bases $\ce{Cl-}$, $\ce{CH3COO-}$, $\ce{CN-}$ and $\ce{OH-}$. Their conjugate acids are HCl (strong), CH₃COOH ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$), HCN ($K_a = 4.9 \times 10^{-10}$) and water. The weakest of these bases is:

options.text_md: $\ce{CH3COO-}$
$\ce{CN-}$
$\ce{Cl-}$
$\ce{OH-}$

questions.solution_md: The stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base. HCl is a strong acid, so Cl⁻ has almost no tendency to take a proton back and is the weakest base — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Water can act both as a Brønsted acid and as a Brønsted base.

**Reason (R):** Water has a high specific heat capacity, about 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. Water donates a proton to NH₃ and accepts one from HCl, so it is amphiprotic. Its specific heat capacity is a true property of water but has nothing to do with proton transfer, so R does not explain A — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Boron trifluoride, BF₃, behaves as a Lewis acid.

**Reason (R):** BF₃ has a lone pair of electrons that it donates to a Lewis base.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: boron has only six electrons in BF₃ and accepts a pair from donors such as NH₃. R is false: BF₃ has no lone pair on boron to donate; it accepts one — option (c).

questions.stem_md: According to the Brønsted–Lowry concept, a base is a substance that can ___ a proton.
questions.solution_md: A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton acceptor.

questions.stem_md: Match each Brønsted acid in Column I with its conjugate base in Column II.

options.text_md: NH₄⁺
HSO₄⁻
H₂O
H₃O⁺

questions.solution_md: The conjugate base is formed by removing one proton from the acid: NH₄⁺ → NH₃, HSO₄⁻ → SO₄²⁻, H₂O → OH⁻, H₃O⁺ → H₂O.

questions.stem_md: Ethanoic acid dissolves in water: $\ce{CH3COOH + H2O <=> CH3COO- + H3O+}$. Identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs.

answer.model_answer_md: CH₃COOH (acid) and CH₃COO⁻ (its conjugate base) form one pair; H₂O (base, it accepts a proton) and H₃O⁺ (its conjugate acid) form the other. The members of each pair differ by one proton.

questions.solution_md: CH₃COOH / CH₃COO⁻ and H₃O⁺ / H₂O.

questions.stem_md: Explain, with one equation for each behaviour, why water is described as amphiprotic.

answer.model_answer_md: Water can donate a proton and so act as an acid: $\ce{NH3 + H2O <=> NH4+ + OH-}$ (acid, with conjugate base OH⁻). It can accept a proton and so act as a base: $\ce{HCl + H2O -> H3O+ + Cl-}$ (base, with conjugate acid H₃O⁺). A substance that can behave as both a Brønsted acid and a Brønsted base is amphiprotic.

questions.solution_md: Acid with NH₃, base with HCl: amphiprotic.

marking_scheme.step: Acid behaviour with a balanced equation
Base behaviour with a balanced equation

questions.stem_md: Classify $\ce{AlCl3}$, $\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{CN-}$ as Lewis acids or Lewis bases, giving the reason for each, and write the equation for the reaction between $\ce{H+}$ and $\ce{NH3}$.

answer.model_answer_md: AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid (incomplete octet; accepts an electron pair). H⁺ is a Lewis acid (empty 1s orbital; accepts a pair). NH₃ is a Lewis base (lone pair on nitrogen to donate). CN⁻ is a Lewis base (lone pair on carbon). $\ce{H+ + NH3 -> NH4+}$: NH₃ donates its lone pair to H⁺, forming a coordinate bond.

questions.solution_md: Acids: AlCl₃, H⁺; bases: NH₃, CN⁻; H⁺ + NH₃ → NH₄⁺.

questions.stem_md: For each reaction in water, name the two conjugate acid–base pairs: (i) $\ce{HSO4- + H2O <=> H3O+ + SO4^2-}$, (ii) $\ce{CH3NH2 + H2O <=> CH3NH3+ + OH-}$, (iii) $\ce{HS- + H2O <=> H2S + OH-}$. State the role of water in each.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) HSO₄⁻ (acid) / SO₄²⁻ (base) and H₃O⁺ (acid) / H₂O (base); water is a base. (ii) CH₃NH₃⁺ (acid) / CH₃NH₂ (base) and H₂O (acid) / OH⁻ (base); water is an acid. (iii) H₂S (acid) / HS⁻ (base) and H₂O (acid) / OH⁻ (base); water is an acid (HS⁻ is the base).

questions.solution_md: Water is a base in (i) and an acid in (ii) and (iii).

(ii) Both pairs and the role of water
(iii) Both pairs and the role of water

questions.stem_md:
(a) State how an acid and a base are defined in the Arrhenius, Brønsted–Lowry and Lewis concepts. [3]

(b) For $\ce{HNO2 + H2O <=> NO2- + H3O+}$ identify the two conjugate acid–base pairs and name one species in the equation that is amphiprotic. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Arrhenius: an acid gives H⁺ (H₃O⁺) in water; a base gives OH⁻ in water. Brønsted–Lowry: an acid is a proton donor; a base is a proton acceptor. Lewis: an acid is an electron-pair acceptor; a base is an electron-pair donor.

(b) HNO₂ (acid) / NO₂⁻ (conjugate base), and H₃O⁺ (conjugate acid) / H₂O (base). Water is amphiprotic (it accepts a proton here and can donate one in other reactions).

questions.solution_md: Three definitions of acid and base; pairs HNO₂/NO₂⁻ and H₃O⁺/H₂O; water amphiprotic.

marking_scheme.step: (b) Water named as amphiprotic with reason

questions.stem_md: A weak monobasic acid is very slightly ionised in a solution of concentration C. The solution is diluted with water to one quarter of this concentration at constant temperature. The degree of ionisation becomes about:

options.text_md: four times its original value
one half of its original value
unchanged
twice its original value

questions.solution_md: For a weak acid α = √(K_a / C). When C falls to C/4, α becomes √(4K_a / C) = 2 × √(K_a / C): the degree of ionisation doubles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: At 298 K, nitrous acid has $K_a = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}$ and benzoic acid has $K_a = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}$. In 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solutions of each, the ratio $[\text{H}^+]$(nitrous acid) to $[\text{H}^+]$(benzoic acid) is about:
questions.solution_md: For a weak acid [H⁺] = √(K_a C), so at equal C the ratio is √(K_a1 / K_a2) = √(4.5 × 10⁻⁴ / 6.5 × 10⁻⁵) = √6.92 = 2.63 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For phosphoric acid, $K_{a1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}$, $K_{a2} = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}$ and $K_{a3} = 4.8 \times 10^{-13}$. The steady fall in the successive values is mainly due to the fact that:

options.text_md: each step has a higher temperature
it is harder to remove a proton from a negatively charged ion than from a neutral molecule
the first proton is held by a covalent bond and the others by ionic bonds
water is used up in the first step

questions.solution_md: Each later proton must leave an anion (H₂PO₄⁻, then HPO₄²⁻) that attracts it electrostatically more strongly than the neutral H₃PO₄ molecule does, so K_a1 ≫ K_a2 ≫ K_a3 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A chemist prepares a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of phosphoric acid in water. Which species are present in appreciable concentrations?

options.text_md: $\ce{H3PO4}$, $\ce{HPO4^2-}$ and $\ce{H+}$, with only traces of $\ce{H2PO4-}$
$\ce{H2PO4-}$, $\ce{HPO4^2-}$, $\ce{PO4^3-}$ and $\ce{H+}$ in equal amounts, with no $\ce{H3PO4}$
$\ce{H3PO4}$, $\ce{H2PO4-}$ and $\ce{H+}$, with only traces of $\ce{HPO4^2-}$ and $\ce{PO4^3-}$
$\ce{PO4^3-}$ and $\ce{H+}$ only

questions.solution_md: K_a1 is much larger than K_a2 and K_a3, so mostly the first ionisation takes place: H₃PO₄ ⇌ H₂PO₄⁻ + H⁺. HPO₄²⁻ and PO₄³⁻ are present only in traces — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution of phosphoric acid, nearly all the hydrogen ions come from the first stage of ionisation.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. K_a1 (7.5 × 10⁻³) is about 10⁵ times K_a2, so the second and third stages add a negligible amount of H⁺.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The degree of ionisation of a weak acid increases when its concentration is increased at constant temperature.

**Reason (R):** The ionisation constant K_a of a weak acid increases on dilution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are false. α = √(K_a / C) falls when C is increased, and K_a depends only on temperature, not on the concentration — option (d).

questions.stem_md: At 298 K, the pH and pOH of any dilute aqueous solution add up to ___.
questions.solution_md: pH + pOH = pK_w = 14 at 298 K.

questions.stem_md: Methanoic acid, HCOOH, has $K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$ at 298 K. Using Ostwald's dilution law with the approximation $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$, calculate the degree of ionisation of a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution.
questions.solution_md: $\alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{C}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1.8 \times 10^{-4}}{0.10}} = \sqrt{1.8 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.042$ (about 4.2%).

questions.stem_md: State Ostwald's dilution law for a weak electrolyte and write the expression that shows how the degree of ionisation depends on the concentration when α is very small.

answer.model_answer_md: Ostwald's dilution law: the degree of ionisation of a weak electrolyte increases on dilution; quantitatively $K = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$, which for $\alpha \ll 1$ gives $\alpha = \sqrt{K/C}$, so α is inversely proportional to the square root of the concentration (directly proportional to √V).

questions.solution_md: K = Cα² / (1 − α); α = √(K/C) for small α.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the acids HCN ($K_a = 4.9 \times 10^{-10}$), CH₃COOH ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$) and HNO₂ ($K_a = 4.5 \times 10^{-4}$) in increasing order of strength, and say which of them has the lowest degree of ionisation at equal concentration.

answer.model_answer_md: A larger K_a means a stronger acid (more ionisation). So the order of increasing strength is HCN < CH₃COOH < HNO₂. At equal concentration α = √(K_a / C), so HCN has the lowest degree of ionisation.

questions.solution_md: HCN < CH₃COOH < HNO₂; HCN has the lowest α.

marking_scheme.step: HCN has the lowest α, using α = √(K_a/C)

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the second ionisation constant of a polybasic acid is much smaller than the first.

answer.model_answer_md: First, the second proton has to be removed from a negatively charged ion, which holds the proton more strongly through electrostatic attraction than the neutral molecule does. Second, the H⁺ ions formed in the first step lower the extent of the second ionisation (the first step has already supplied H⁺ to the solution, so the second step is held back).

questions.solution_md: Proton removal from an anion is harder; H⁺ from the first step suppresses the second step.

questions.stem_md: Write the three stages of ionisation of phosphoric acid in water with their ionisation constants ($7.5 \times 10^{-3}$, $6.2 \times 10^{-8}$ and $4.8 \times 10^{-13}$), and explain which stage supplies almost all the hydrogen ions.

answer.model_answer_md: $\ce{H3PO4 <=> H+ + H2PO4-}$, $K_{a1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}$; $\ce{H2PO4- <=> H+ + HPO4^2-}$, $K_{a2} = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}$; $\ce{HPO4^2- <=> H+ + PO4^3-}$, $K_{a3} = 4.8 \times 10^{-13}$. Since $K_{a1} \gg K_{a2} \gg K_{a3}$ (each about 10⁵ times smaller), the first stage supplies almost all the hydrogen ions; the later stages add a negligible amount.

questions.solution_md: Three stages with K_a1 ≫ K_a2 ≫ K_a3; first stage gives nearly all H⁺.

marking_scheme.step: Second and third stages with their constants
First stage gives nearly all H⁺ because K_a1 ≫ K_a2 ≫ K_a3

questions.stem_md: Ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K) is prepared at 0.040 mol L⁻¹ and then diluted four-fold to 0.010 mol L⁻¹. Calculate its degree of ionisation in each solution using α = √(Ka/C), and state what the ratio shows.

(a) For a weak monobasic acid HA of concentration C mol L⁻¹ and degree of ionisation α, derive Ostwald's dilution law $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$ and the simplified form for a very weak acid. [3]

(b) Calculate the degree of ionisation and the hydrogen ion concentration of 0.040 mol L⁻¹ benzoic acid ($K_a = 6.5 \times 10^{-5}$). [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}$. Initially C of HA; at equilibrium HA: $C(1-\alpha)$, H⁺: $C\alpha$, A⁻: $C\alpha$.
$K_a = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]} = \dfrac{C\alpha \cdot C\alpha}{C(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1-\alpha}$.
For a very weak acid α ≪ 1, so $1 - \alpha \approx 1$, $K_a = C\alpha^2$ and $\alpha = \sqrt{K_a/C}$. So α decreases as C increases (increases on dilution).

(b) $\alpha = \sqrt{6.5 \times 10^{-5}/0.040} = \sqrt{1.625 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.0403$; $[\text{H}^+] = C\alpha = 0.040 \times 0.0403 = 1.6 × 10⁻³$ mol L⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Equilibrium amounts C(1 − α), Cα, Cα

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the three stages of ionisation of phosphoric acid and the expression for $K_{a1}$. [2]

(b) For a 0.10 mol L⁻¹ solution, $K_{a1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-3}$, $K_{a2} = 6.2 \times 10^{-8}$ (given as before). Calculate $[\text{H}^+]$ from the first stage alone, by solving $\dfrac{x^2}{0.10 - x} = K_{a1}$, and the pH. [2]

(c) Explain why the second stage may be neglected. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) $\ce{H3PO4 <=> H+ + H2PO4-}$, $\ce{H2PO4- <=> H+ + HPO4^2-}$, $\ce{HPO4^2- <=> H+ + PO4^3-}$; $K_{a1} = \dfrac{[\text{H}^+][\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]}{[\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4]}$.

(b) $x^2 + 7.5 \times 10^{-3}x - 7.5 \times 10^{-4} = 0$, so $x = 0.0239$ mol L⁻¹ = [H⁺]; pH = −log(0.0239) = 1.62.

(c) $K_{a2}$ is about 10⁵ times smaller than $K_{a1}$, so the extra [H⁺] from the second stage (about 6 × 10⁻⁸ mol L⁻¹) is negligible beside 0.024 mol L⁻¹.

marking_scheme.step: (c) K_a2 ≪ K_a1, so the second stage adds negligible H⁺

questions.stem_md: The ionic product of water is $K_w = 5.5 \times 10^{-14}$ at 323 K (given). The pH of pure water at 323 K, and its nature, are:

options.text_md: 6.63, acidic
7.00, neutral
7.00, acidic
6.63, neutral

questions.solution_md: In pure water [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = √K_w = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.3 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹, so pH = 6.63. Since [H⁺] = [OH⁻] the water is still neutral; neutrality is at pH = ½ pK_w, not always 7 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In a laboratory, 10.0 mL of 0.10 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid is made up to 1.0 L with water. The pH of the diluted solution at 298 K is:
questions.solution_md: Moles of HCl = 0.10 × 0.0100 = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol in 1.0 L, so [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ and pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3.00 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Sulphuric acid solution of concentration 0.0050 mol L⁻¹ is taken, and both protons are assumed to be completely ionised. The pH at 298 K is:
A solution of hydrochloric acid has a concentration of 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ at 298 K. Its pOH is:
questions.solution_md: pH = −log(1.0 × 10⁻³) = 3, and pH + pOH = 14 at 298 K, so pOH = 11 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Mixing 25.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid with 25.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution gives a mixture whose pH at 298 K is:
questions.solution_md: n(H⁺) = 25.0 × 0.200 = 5.00 mmol and n(OH⁻) = 25.0 × 0.100 = 2.50 mmol. The excess H⁺ is 2.50 mmol in 50.0 mL, so [H⁺] = 0.050 mol L⁻¹ and pH = 1.30 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The pH of a 0.050 mol L⁻¹ solution of ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K), assuming α is small, is about:
Lemon juice has a pH of 2.5 and milk has a pH of 6.5. The hydrogen ion concentration of the lemon juice is how many times that of milk?
questions.solution_md: A difference of 4 pH units is a factor of 10⁴ in [H⁺] because pH is a logarithmic scale: the ratio of [H⁺] in lemon juice to [H⁺] in milk is 10^(6.5 − 2.5) = 10⁴ — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The pH of 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid at 298 K is 3.0.

**Reason (R):** pH is defined as the negative of the natural logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: A is true: [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ gives pH 3.0. R is false: pH is defined with the logarithm to base 10 (pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]), not the natural logarithm — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A neutral aqueous solution has a pH of exactly 7 at every temperature.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻]. Since K_w changes with temperature, so does the pH of neutrality (for example 6.63 at 323 K).

questions.stem_md: A technician prepares a 0.020 mol L⁻¹ solution of barium hydroxide, a strong base that is completely ionised, at 298 K. Calculate its pH.

marking_scheme.step: [OH⁻] = 0.040 mol L⁻¹ (two OH⁻ per formula unit)

questions.stem_md: In an acid–base experiment, 40.0 mL of 0.150 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid and 25.0 mL of 0.200 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide are mixed at 298 K. Calculate the pH of the mixture.

questions.stem_md: A cleaning solution in a Pune laboratory contains aqueous ammonia at 0.30 mol L⁻¹. Taking Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ at 298 K and α ≪ 1, calculate the pH of the solution.
The ionic product of water is 5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² L⁻² at 323 K (given). Calculate the pH of pure water at 323 K.
questions.solution_md: In pure water [H⁺] = √K_w = √(5.5 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.35 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹, so pH = 6.63.

questions.stem_md: Define the ionic product of water and state its value at 298 K. Why does it increase with temperature?

answer.model_answer_md: The ionic product of water is $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-]$, the product of the molar concentrations of hydrogen and hydroxide ions in water or any dilute aqueous solution; at 298 K, $K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ mol² L⁻². The self-ionisation of water is endothermic, so a rise in temperature favours ionisation and increases K_w.

questions.solution_md: K_w = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; increases because ionisation is endothermic.

questions.stem_md: Define pH. A sample of rainwater has a hydrogen ion concentration of 3.2 × 10⁻⁴ mol L⁻¹ at 298 K; calculate its pH and pOH.

answer.model_answer_md: pH is the negative logarithm (to base 10) of the hydrogen ion concentration in mol L⁻¹: pH = −log[H⁺]. For the rainwater pH = −log(3.2 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.49, and pOH = 14 − 3.49 = 10.51.

questions.stem_md: A student mixes 30.0 mL of 0.250 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide with 20.0 mL of 0.300 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid at 298 K. Find the pH of the mixture and say whether it is acidic, basic or neutral.

answer.model_answer_md: n(OH⁻) = 30.0 × 0.250 = 7.50 mmol; n(H⁺) = 20.0 × 0.300 = 6.00 mmol. Excess OH⁻ = 1.50 mmol in 50.0 mL, so [OH⁻] = 0.030 mol L⁻¹, pOH = 1.52 and pH = 14 − 1.52 = 12.48. The mixture is basic.

questions.solution_md: pH = 12.48; basic.

marking_scheme.step: Moles of OH⁻ and H⁺ with the excess (1.50 mmol)

questions.stem_md: At 373 K the ionic product of water is 5.1 × 10⁻¹³ (given). (i) Calculate the pH of pure water at this temperature and justify that it is still neutral. (ii) Calculate the pH of 0.010 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide at 373 K.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = √(5.1 × 10⁻¹³) = 7.1 × 10⁻⁷ mol L⁻¹, so pH = 6.15. The concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ are equal, so the water is neutral although its pH is below 7. (ii) pK_w = 12.29; pOH = 2.00, so pH = pK_w − pOH = 12.29 − 2.00 = 10.29.

questions.stem_md: Calculate the degree of ionisation and the pH of a 0.25 mol L⁻¹ solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 × 10⁻⁴ at 298 K), using α = √(Ka/C).

A 20.0 mL portion of 0.50 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide solution is diluted with water to a total volume of 1.0 L at 298 K. Calculate the pH of the solution before and after dilution, and the factor by which [OH⁻] falls.

answer.model_answer_md: Before: [OH⁻] = 0.50 mol L⁻¹, pOH = 0.30, pH = 13.70. After: n(OH⁻) = 0.50 × 0.0200 = 0.010 mol in 1.0 L, so [OH⁻] = 0.010 mol L⁻¹, pOH = 2.00 and pH = 12.00. [OH⁻] falls by a factor of 50 (0.50 / 0.010), but the pH changes by only 1.70 units.

questions.solution_md: pH 13.70 before, 12.00 after; factor 50.

marking_scheme.step: Factor of 50 and the logarithmic scale

(a) Write the relation between pH, pOH and pK_w, and give the value of pK_w at 298 K. [1]

(b) Calculate the pH at 298 K of a 0.0020 mol L⁻¹ solution of barium hydroxide, which is completely ionised. [2]

(c) Calculate the pH of a 0.020 mol L⁻¹ solution of ethanoic acid ($K_a = 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$), assuming $\alpha \ll 1$. [2]

questions.stem_md: An acid–base indicator is a weak organic acid HIn whose un-ionised form and ion In⁻ have different colours. Its colour changes over a narrow range because:

options.text_md: the ratio [In⁻]/[HIn] changes from about 1/10 to 10 over roughly one pH unit on each side of its pK
the indicator reacts completely with the first drop of acid
the indicator ionises completely at pH 7 in all solutions
the indicator changes the pH of the solution by two units

questions.solution_md: In HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻ the ratio of the two coloured forms depends on [H⁺]. One colour dominates when the ratio is 10 or more, the other when it is 0.1 or less, so the visible change takes place over about 2 pH units around pK_In — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid against 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide. The best indicator for the end point is:

options.text_md: methyl orange (pH range 3.1–4.4)
methyl red (pH range 4.4–6.2)
phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3–10.0)
litmus paper alone, since it gives a clear colour

questions.solution_md: The solution at the equivalence point contains the sodium salt of a weak acid and its pH is about 8.7, above 7. Phenolphthalein, which changes between pH 8.3 and 10.0, changes colour sharply at this point — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A student titrates 0.1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid against 0.1 mol L⁻¹ aqueous ammonia and looks for a suitable indicator. The best choice is:

options.text_md: methyl orange (pH range 3.1–4.4) or methyl red (pH range 4.4–6.2)
phenolphthalein (pH range 8.3–10.0)
bromothymol blue (pH range 6.0–7.6) only
any indicator, since the pH change is vertical over the whole range

questions.solution_md: The equivalence point lies at a pH below 7, so the indicator must change colour in the acidic range, near pH 3–6.5. Methyl orange and methyl red do; phenolphthalein would change colour only after the equivalence point had been passed by a large margin — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the titration of 0.1 mol L⁻¹ hydrochloric acid against 0.1 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide, the pH changes sharply from about 4 to about 10 near the equivalence point. This means that:

options.text_md: only phenolphthalein can be used
only methyl orange can be used
both methyl orange and phenolphthalein can be used, since their ranges lie within the steep part of the curve
no indicator can be used

questions.solution_md: Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) and phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) change colour within a tiny volume of titrant on the near-vertical section of the curve, so either gives an accurate end point — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Methyl orange is red below pH 3.1 and yellow above pH 4.4. Its colour in a solution of pH 8 is:

options.text_md: yellow
red
orange
colourless

questions.solution_md: pH 8 is well above the upper end (4.4) of the colour-change range, so only the yellow (basic) form is seen — option (a).

questions.stem_md: It is found that no ordinary indicator gives a sharp end point in the titration of a weak acid against a weak base because:

options.text_md: the equivalence point lies exactly at pH 14
the pH changes only gradually near the equivalence point, with no steep rise
weak acids and bases react only in the presence of a catalyst
the pH at equivalence is below zero

questions.solution_md: In a weak acid–weak base titration there is no sharp vertical jump in the curve, so the colour of an indicator changes over many millilitres of titrant instead of one drop — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for the titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide.

**Reason (R):** At the equivalence point the solution is basic, with a pH within the colour-change range of phenolphthalein.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion.
Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true. The equivalence point is at about pH 8.7, which lies in the range 8.3–10.0 of phenolphthalein, and R gives the reason for A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: What is an acid–base indicator? Why is only a few drops of it added in a titration?

answer.model_answer_md: An indicator is a weak organic acid or base whose ionised and un-ionised forms have different colours, so its colour changes over a narrow pH range (about pK ± 1) near the end point. Only a few drops are used because the indicator is itself an acid or base and would use up some of the titrant, causing an error in the end point.

questions.solution_md: Weak acid or base with two colours; few drops because it consumes titrant.

Few drops: otherwise it uses up titrant

questions.stem_md: Hydrochloric acid is titrated with aqueous ammonia. Which indicator would you choose between methyl orange (3.1–4.4) and phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0)? Give two reasons, referring to the pH at the equivalence point.

answer.model_answer_md: Methyl orange. The end point of a strong acid–weak base titration lies below pH 7 (about 5.3 for 0.1 mol L⁻¹ solutions), so the indicator must change colour in the acidic range; methyl orange changes at 3.1–4.4, close to the steep part of the curve. Phenolphthalein changes at 8.3–10.0, which is far above the equivalence point on a curve that is nearly flat there, so it would give an end point that is not sharp and has a large error.

questions.solution_md: Methyl orange: end point at pH below 7; phenolphthalein is unsuitable.

marking_scheme.step: Equivalence point pH below 7 matches the range 3.1–4.4
Phenolphthalein would not give a sharp end point

questions.stem_md:
A student titrates 25.0 mL of 0.100 mol L⁻¹ ethanoic acid with 0.100 mol L⁻¹ sodium hydroxide and calculates the following pH values (data given):

| Volume of NaOH / mL | 0 | 12.5 | 24.9 | 25.0 | 25.1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pH | 2.88 | 4.75 | 7.14 | 8.72 | 10.30 |

(a) Calculate the volume of sodium hydroxide at the equivalence point and say, from the table, whether the solution there is acidic, basic or neutral. [2]

(b) Between which pH values does the curve rise steeply, and which indicator, methyl orange (3.1–4.4), bromothymol blue (6.0–7.6) or phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0), would you use? [2]

(c) Explain why methyl orange would be unsuitable. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The equivalence point is at 25.0 mL of NaOH (equal moles of acid and base, 25.0 × 0.100 = 2.50 mmol each). The pH there is 8.72, so the solution is basic.

(b) The curve rises steeply from about 7.1 (24.9 mL) to about 10.3 (25.1 mL). Phenolphthalein (8.3–10.0) changes colour within this steep part, so it is used.

(c) Methyl orange changes colour at pH 3.1–4.4, well before the equivalence point, on the gently sloping part of the curve where the pH changes slowly (it would change over many millilitres), so the end point would be seen too early and not sharply.

questions.solution_md: (a) 25.0 mL; pH 8.72; basic. (b) phenolphthalein.
